abstract: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis is widely used to generate hypotheses and interpret findings, reducing the time and effort required for manual literature searches and evidence curation. However, how closely these methods recover effortful expert-curated syntheses has not been established. We present NeuroMetaBench, an openly available benchmark linking expert curation records across stages of systematic review, from author-stated eligibility criteria and research-article inclusion decisions to individual analysis selections and meta-analysis-specific reference maps. The resource includes bibliographic records for 1,611 research-article inclusions across 17 quantitative review articles and candidate search pools for three. For nine review articles, it also provides analysis-level selections and coordinate data across 35 meta-analyses, documenting which reported results contributed to each meta-analysis and enabling reproducible construction of standardized reference maps. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating three established automated methods: Neurosynth, NeuroQuery, and NeuroVLM. Across the benchmark, automated maps generally showed limited to moderate spatial correspondence with expert-curated reference maps, with substantial variation across meta-analysis topics and characteristics. NeuroMetaBench provides an openly available, community-driven resource for evaluating established automated meta-analysis methods, and is well positioned to evaluate emerging LLM-based approaches to automated neuroimaging synthesis.
